article_text:
Pour sa deuxième édition, le prix du Livre Robert Delpire a récompensé le projet Caty, la vie, la mort , de Caty Jan et Mat Jacob. L’ouvrage sortira chez Delpire en fin d’année 2027.

« Le Prix a été attribué à une œuvre unique, singulière et tragique. Un travail à quatre mains et en deux volumes, le premier, inédit, le second, intime et hanté. Caty, la vie, la mort , le titre le dit avec souffrance et tremblement » , déclare Sarah Moon dans le communiqué diffusé à l’occasion de la remise du prix du Livre Robert Delpire. La photographe en présidait le jury composé de Quentin Bajac , directeur du Jeu de Paume, José Chidlovsky, réalisateur, Michel Christolhomme, président de Pour que l’esprit vive, Héloïse Conesa, chargée de la collection de photographie contemporaine au département des Estampes et de la Photographie de la BnF, Emmanuelle Kouchner, directrice des éditions Delpire, Wajdi Mouawad, metteur en scène et écrivain, et Natacha Wolinski, écrivaine et critique. Chacun des membres a proposé et défendu un projet de livre avant de s’accorder sur celui Caty Jan et Mat Jacob, qui devient ainsi le deuxième à obtenir la récompense.

Un regard sur l’existence

Caty, la vie, la mort se distingue par sa genèse poignante. Caty Jan et Mat Jacob se sont rencontrés en 1989. Animés par une passion commune pour le 8e art, ils se lient d’une amitié qui deviendra une histoire d’amour et donnera naissance à un enfant. Aux côtés d’autres photographes, ils cofondent le collectif Tendance Floue , en 1991, et multiplient les projets. Seulement, en 2003, Caty Jan est victime d’un accident vasculaire cérébral. « Elle perd l’usage de la parole, se retrouve emmurée dans un corps accidenté. Elle ne photographiera plus. Elle garde cependant une extrême lucidité, une sensibilité, et son regard sur la vie » , explique Mat Jacob dans sa note d’intention.

Dans le souvenir de sa compagne, disparue en novembre 2025, celui-ci a imaginé ce projet présenté au prix du Livre Robert Delpire. « Depuis qu’elle est partie, avec la force qu’ont les défunts de résister à l’absence, le projet de composer un livre à quatre mains, les siennes, les miennes, ne me quitte pas. Un livre sur les liens qui nous définissent, qui nous obligent, les chemins que nous empruntons, la fragilité, la création, la liberté et le temps qui passe » , poursuit-il. Mêlant textes et images, Caty, la vie, la mort témoignera du parcours de l’autrice, de son œuvre comme de son existence. Il s’agira de son premier ouvrage.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Emmy-nominated This is Us star Chris Sullivan has joined Jeremy Holm ( House of Cards , Mr. Robot ) on thriller Tessellation as production gets underway in Illinois.

The feature directorial debut of screenwriter Michael Moreci follows disgraced puzzle champion and CIA codebreaker Anton (Holm) who is drawn into a conspiracy that forces him to confront the one code he could never crack: the reason his wife had to die.

The cast also features Stephen Louis Grush ( The Righteous Gemstones ) and Winter Williams ( The Human Centipede ).

Madeleine Coghlan To Topline Horror Film 'Puppet' From Nick Peterson; Chris Sullivan, Taryn Manning & Kevin Keppy Also Set

“ Tessellation is very much a movie for our times,” said Moreci. “Nothing is real, fringe paranoia has become mainstream, and we’re losing our ability to even verify the truth.

Watch on Deadline

“We’re following in the footsteps of The Conversation , Blow Out , and The Parallax View , movies that also dealt with paranoia and distrust, and I’m proud to carry forward the tradition of these important films.”

Moreci has won acclaim for his work spanning comics, film and television. His breakout comedic dark fantasy comic series Barbaric has sold more than one million copies and is currently in development as a series at Netflix. Other notable screenwriting credits include the Shudder horror film Revealer and Revival for Syfy/Peacock.

Tessellation is produced by Robert Patrick Stern, Kevin Lau and Moreci, as well as Stephen Mastrocola, in association with Static Films. Damian Wassel, Jen Shelby, Rhett Bruno and Steven Beaulieu of Aethon Books serve as executive producers. Stephanie Slife is the line producer.

“Static Films is built on the philosophy of supporting artists early in their careers, because Hollywood doesn’t always know what it wants until they see it. The low-budget debuts of Christopher Nolan ( Following ), Darren Aronofsky ( Pi ), and more recently, Jane Schoenbrun ( We’re All Going to the World’s Fair ) serve as both inspiration and reminders of where these filmmakers can go,” said Mastrocola.

“When I first read Tessellation , I was immediately compelled by Michael’s vision, the script’s unique structure, and how relevant it is in these strange times. We’re looking forward to seeing if audiences can solve Anton’s puzzle when it comes to theaters next year.”

Holm is represented by Formation Talent Agency and Prevail Artist Entertainment. Grush is represented by Stewart Talent, LTA and Robert Stein Management. Sullivan is represented by Gersh and Suskin/Karshan Management.

Cameras are set to roll this week at Flyover Film Studios in Central Illinois.

article_text:
Nearly a year after “ Heated Rivalry ” debuted on streaming, fans are venturing to movie theaters to rewatch the steamy romance between hockey superstars Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie).

The limited theatrical release, which is scheduled from Nov. 6 through Nov. 30, has generated $1.4 million from 945 theaters, according to distributor Regal Entertainment. Moviegoers were able to choose between three paired screenings (episodes 1 and 2: “Rookies” and “Olympians”, episodes 3 and 4: “Hunter” and “Rose,” and episodes 5 and 6: “I’ll Believe in Anything” and “The Cottage”), with tickets for each showtime costing $9.99. That’s less than the average movie price, which is $12.87 for standard screenings, according to research firm EntTelligence.

Related Stories

It’s an impressive haul for a show that’s widely available to stream at home. There aren’t many points of comparison at the box office. When television shows like Netflix’s “Stranger Things” series finale or the Christian drama “The Chosen” have played on the big screen, they aired new, never-before-seen episodes. Although Netflix didn’t report grosses for “Stranger Things,” the Season 5 series finale was estimated to have earned a massive $25 million to $28 million around New Year’s Eve. However, that’s not a fair reference given the super-sized, two-hour finale was the much-anticipated conclusion to the streamer’s biggest series of all time. In any case, theatrical releases or (re-releases) of popular TV shows are all gravy for cinema operators, who are enjoying the biggest year at the box office since the onset of the pandemic. Gen Z, the target demographic for shows like “Heated Rivalry,” has been driving the movie theater resurgence .

“This could become a really interesting trend, not only as a way to bring fans together but also to keep popular series top of mind during gaps between seasons, when maintaining momentum can be a challenge,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. “We initially thought this might be something largely confined to the faith-based space, but clearly the potential extends to virtually any series with a passionate fan base.”

He adds, “Of course, not every television series is going to translate into a successful big-screen event, but for the right show with the right audience, movie theaters could become an exciting extension of the television experience rather than simply an alternative to it.”

“Heated Rivalry,” based on Rachel Reid’s “Game Changers” book series, is gearing up for a second season. The Canadian-produced show was released in the U.S. on HBO Max in November 2025, although it didn’t become a word-of-mouth sensation until early 2026, when episodes reached an average viewership of more than 10 million and made instant stars out of Williams and Storrie.

“When a series connects with audiences the way ‘Heated Rivalry’ has, we look for ways to bring it to the big screen and give fans a reason to experience it together,” Regal’s senior VP of U.S. content Brooks LeBoeuf said prior to the re-release. “It’s a chance to celebrate the story, its creators and its performances before Season 2 arrives in 2027.”

article_text:
For those of us fatigued by the carnivorous cycle perpetuated by narratives and images of police brutality, Geeta Gandbhir’s latest, The Perfect Neighbor , functions as a balm. Which is not to say that this is a feel-good film —Gandbhir’s chillingly detailed documentary tracks a story that unfolded over 16 months in an inland Florida town, and ended in the demise of Ajike Owens, a beloved Black mother of four, at the hands of her white neighbor, Susan Lorincz, who was emboldened by racist paranoia and Florida’s controversial stand-your-ground laws.

But The Perfect Neighbor achieves a kind of reclamation. The documentary is assembled almost entirely from body-camera footage recorded by the cops whom Lorincz frequently called to the neighborhood, in an attempt to restrict her Black neighbors and their kids from living their lives and enjoying public space. Local law enforcement’s presence on the scene was thus near constant—but Gandbhir draws our attention to the gaps in their footage. When the only real moment of violence occurs, as Lorincz shoots Owens through a closed door, there are no police or cameras around. In inverting the use of technologies intended for state surveillance, Gandbhir delivers a subtle yet powerful critique of the failures of institutions that purport to protect us.

Last January, shortly after the world premiere of The Perfect Neighbor at the Sundance Film Festival, I spoke with Gandbhir about the making of the film , her personal connection to the story, and her subversion of the true-crime genre.

Can you tell me about the first time you became aware of this story?

Ajike Owens was a close friend of Kim, my sister-in-law, who lives in Ocala [Florida]. They were raising their kids together, celebrating birthdays together, all that sort of stuff. They were each other’s family. So when Ajike was killed, we got a call from Kim’s sister, Tameka, who is an activist and organizer. She was returning from Jamaica, but her plane was diverted to New York because of the weather. My husband and I picked her up, and after hearing her story, we told her she wasn’t going alone. We got on a plane and went down to Florida with her.

We decided to start filming because we were really concerned that Susan would not be arrested due to Florida’s stand-your-ground laws. We wanted to make the media aware of the suppression going on with local authorities, and make sure justice for Ajike was a possibility. When she was finally arrested four days later, we remained concerned that she would be set free by a jury, because, again, Florida’s stand-your-ground laws are often weaponized against people of color. White people use it as a license to kill. The legal team did a FOIA request for all the materials the police department had, which then became public record. That’s when we first saw the body-camera footage, and we realized that it went back two years. Susan had been calling the police on the community for two years.

So we went through all the footage. Originally, we were trying to use it to help the legal team, but in watching it, I realized that this was the film . The footage paints a portrait of the community before the tragedy. Being that there’s so much gun violence in this country, unfortunately, we often see the aftermath of a shooting but not what the community was like before. For us, that was critical. Police body-cam footage is used to surveil communities of color in order to protect the police, so we wanted to flip that on its head and use it to show the point of view of this community—this tight-knit, diverse community of families just living their lives, being joyful, and taking care of each other.

Knowing that there’s this familial connection behind the film adds another texture to it.

We thought we would do a film that followed the family for a year and their attempts to get justice and impact change. But to be honest, I also made this film to mitigate our grief. We wanted to understand what had happened for ourselves. It’s only been a year and a half [since Owens’s murder], and we’re still grieving. It was a way to put purpose to the pain.

What makes the film so effective are your deliberate choices to establish the constant police presence in the neighborhood—and then there’s this absence of the police during the one actual moment of crime. That gap in the footage is really palpable.

The only person who ever called the police into that community was Susan. This is a community that has experienced systemic racism and the bias in policing; this is a community that never called the cops. It would not be their choice. Ajike tried several times to do what neighbors do to resolve disputes and talk directly with Susan, and she was greeted with hostility every time. My opinion is that the police had dismissed Susan as a nuisance, and so she took matters into her own hands. I think she thought that she would walk, you know? Again, these are really dangerous laws that embolden people. It’s not just in Florida; there are other states where castle doctrines exist and are part of the legal framework. It’s mostly used by white people against Black and brown folks. I believe that’s what happened here.

There’s a growing trend on YouTube where people take a similar approach to that of your movie, and catalogue and time-stamp police body-camera footage to track a crime story. Were you aware of this trend before?

No. I’d seen crime interrogations online. There are organizations like Witness that use such footage, and there’s also a film , Incident (2023), that uses body-camera footage. But because crime was not the focus for me, I didn’t think about it in that way.

Popular documentaries now exist in two categories: celebrity biopic and true crime. Your film adds a wrinkle to the true-crime genre. Was that a conscious choice?

I do not think of this film as true crime. This is a story that happened to my family, and I made it to mitigate grief. One of my concerns coming to Sundance was that I wasn’t sure there was a place for it in the world, because it can’t be categorized. You’re making something that hasn’t been seen before, and that can also be problematic in this culture where so much is algorithm-based. I wasn’t too interested in the commerciality of this; I just wanted this story out somehow.

One year after making this, I showed it to Ajike’s mother, Pamela [Dias]. She was a witness every step of the way, we never would have done this without her permission—but I warned her it would be really hard, and she didn’t have to watch this. We could just shelve it. We could put this out into the world because it makes an impact—or we could forget it, and it’ll just have been my process, me doing something to help me get through this moment. But Pamela is the bravest person I know. She watched it, and managed to get through it. I think it took her a while, but she said she wanted to try to put it out into the world. She takes a lot of strength from Mamie Till, Emmett Till’s mother. There’s a lot of traumatic stuff there, but her attitude is the same: the world needs to see what happened to my baby. The way Emmett Till’s mother had an open casket at his funeral after he was lynched, so people could see what happened to him.

The film ends with Susan’s trial, which wrapped up in late 2024. Did you always want to end with that final verdict?

No, as you know, trials often get pushed. There’s no schedule to them. It was supposed to be in June, and then it was pushed to August. Originally, we thought it was going to be in November or December of 2023. Once Susan was arrested, which you saw was the most ridiculous kind of circus, with her refusing to leave the room—once that had happened, we thought that we could end the film there. We could have a title card saying that the trial was pending, and hopefully that would keep people engaged. It just so happened that the trial happened in time to add it in. At one point I questioned whether we should interweave the trial throughout the film , and I thought, absolutely not. It is a full story up until the arrest—and then the family gets to have the last word.

You’ve talked about how the film was a kind of “grief work” for you. I’m wondering: do you have a great hope for the film ?

The hope is always very lofty: to change some of these laws that put so many people’s lives in danger, especially those of people of color. I believe there are 700 deaths a year due to stand-your-ground laws. That’s 700 people who could still be alive, and that’s important to me.

And I would love to fulfill Ajike’s wish for her legacy; that’s sort of my mission. This may sound crazy, but I think I talked to her in my dreams. I want her to rest and to feel that her children are cared for. I want her to know we’re carrying on in her name.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "2B Galerie的展览呈现了约30幅并非传统摄影的照片；它们不是直觉或印象的产物，而是理念与实验的结晶。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿兰·弗莱舍（Alain Fleischer）父亲具有匈牙利血统，是一位法国跨学科艺术家、电影人兼作家。他的作品打破了古典摄影的法典：他的图像既不是直觉或转瞬即逝的印象的产物，而是深思熟虑的概念与严谨实验的成果。对他而言，摄影不是一件固定的作品，而是一种可资塑造的可塑材料。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿兰·弗莱舍的摄影作品主要以对倒影、光学幻觉和夜间光线投影的实验为特征。在20世纪70年代初的首次公开亮相中，他以一种将裸体模特身体与投射其上的影像相结合的创新技术（《身体-银幕》“Corps-écrans”，1970–1971年）吸引了法国摄影界的关注。在后来的系列《面孔之夜》（“La Nuit des visages”，1995年）中，他没有借助暗室蒙太奇或数字修图，而是在夜间将女性面孔的幻灯片直接投射到树干或岩石上。通过长时间曝光拍摄出的照片，借助背景中过滤的月光，创造出一种神秘的图像。他20世纪80年代的照片展现了人们在各种日常金属物品（如勺子、茶壶或熨斗）中的倒影，将它们转化为虚幻、神秘的面孔（《银器与其他倒影》“Argenterie et autres reflets”）。倒影和运动的运用也在他1981年的系列作品《镜子-抽屉》（“Miroirs-Tiroirs”）中再次出现。他捕捉了嵌镜抽屉被拉开的那一刻。其结果揭示了一种肉眼无法看到的运动和倒影图像。在《美好日子》（“Happy Days”）系列中，则是古典绘画中的模特，通过玩具拉动的镜子反射，从画作中被剥离出来并变成摄影作品。名为《我只是一张图像》（“Je ne suis qu’une image”）的装置艺术构思于2017年，旨在将声音转化为图像。其雕塑版本在巴黎卡门广场音乐学院（Conservatoire de musique, place Carmen）门外的户外部署。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2B Galerie的展览向公众展出了揭示摄影无限可能并为不同视觉方法开辟道路的作品。除了大约30幅照片外，展览还包括几部短片，同样证明了弗莱舍创作过程的多样性、创造力以及取之不尽的奇思妙想。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿兰·弗莱舍，实验的冒险家 2026年11月3日 – 12月20日 2B Galerie 匈牙利布达佩斯1092拉代街47号（Ráday u. 47） https://2b-org.hu/", "links": [{"text": "https://2b-org.hu/", "url": "https://2b-org.hu/"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
The exhibition at 2B Galerie presents some thirty photos that are not conventional photographs; they are not the result of intuition or impressions, but of ideas and experiments.

Of Hungarian descent on his father’s side, Alain Fleischer is a French multidisciplinary artist, filmmaker and writer. His work breaks free from the codes of classical photography: his images are the product neither of intuition nor of fleeting impression, but of carefully considered concepts and rigorous experiments. For him, photography is not a fixed work but a malleable material to be shaped.

Alain Fleischer’s photographic work is characterized mainly by experiments with reflections, optical illusions and nocturnal light projections. In the early 1970s, at his first public appearances, he drew the attention of the French photographic world with an innovative technique of dressing his nude models in images projected onto the body (“Corps-écrans”, 1970–1971). In a later series, “La Nuit des visages” (1995), instead of resorting to laboratory montage or digital retouching, he projected slides of female faces at night directly onto a tree trunk or a rock. The shot, taken with a long exposure time, creates a mystical image thanks to moonlight filtered in the background. His photographs of the 1980s show the reflections of people in various everyday metal objects such as a spoon, a teapot or an iron, transforming them into unreal, mysterious faces (“Argenterie et autres reflets”). The use of reflection and movement can be found again in his 1981 series “Miroirs-Tiroirs”. He captures the moment when mirror-lined drawers are opened. The result reveals an image of a movement and a reflection that it would be impossible to see with the naked eye. In the series “Happy Days”, it is the models of old paintings, reflected by mirrors pulled by toys, that are extracted from the paintings to become photographs. The installation entitled “Je ne suis qu’une image”, which transforms sound into image, was conceived in 2017. A sculptural version was erected outdoors, in front of the Conservatoire de musique, place Carmen, in Paris.

The exhibition at 2B Galerie presents to the public works that reveal the unlimited possibilities of photography and open the way to a different visual approach. In addition to some thirty photographs, the exhibition also includes a few short videos, which likewise testify to the diversity of his working processes, to Fleischer’s creativity and to his inexhaustible wealth of ideas.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Tomorrow brings the start of a Winnipeg shoot for Homesick , an indie horror thriller to star Mena Suvari ( American Beauty ), David Arquette ( Scream franchise), Belle Shouse (Netflix’s Monsters: The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story ) and Alberto Rosende ( Chicago Fire ).

From Evoke Entertainment and Freefall Films , the film revolves around Suvari’s Dr. Abby Morrison, a compassionate physician whose carefully built life conceals a secret she has never shared with her husband. With their daughter away at college, Abby and husband Gordy (Arquette) are settling into life as empty nesters when the arrival of a mysterious young woman (Shouse) shatters their sense of safety. As an unsettling encounter spirals into a nightmare, the couple must fight to protect each other in a home they can no longer trust.

Todd Slavkin , a veteran of shows like Shadowhunters , The Mysterious Benedict Society and Smallville , is directing from a script written with longtime writing and producing partner Darren Swimmer. Stan Spry, Henry Boger and Anthony Fankhauser are producing; Jeff Holland, Geoff Silverman, Slavkin and Swimmer are exec producing; and Pam Mitchell is co-producing.

Watch on Deadline

Slavkin and Swimmer are repped by Evoke Entertainment, IAG, and Gendler, Kelly & Cunningham. Suvari is repped by Innovative, Management Production Entertainment, and Jackoway Austen Tyerman; Arquette by Artium Talent, Lighthouse Entertainment, and Brecheen Feldman. Breimer; Shouse by Innovative, Industry Entertainment, and Meyer & Downs; and Rosende by Yorn, Levine, Barnes.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Oscar nominee Sam Pollard ’s documentary Tutu , about the late archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize winner Desmond Tutu, will soon be arriving in theaters.

Freestyle Releasing plans to open the film in the U.S. on December 18. Tutu , winner of the Cinema for Peace Award at the 2026 Berlinale where it also earned a Special Mention for the festival’s Documentary Award, opens in the UK on December 11. It examines the life and work of the Archbishop of Cape Town who became a leading figure in the successful effort to dismantle South Africa’s racist Apartheid policies and bring down the white supremacist regime.

Related Stories

“Desmond Tutu was more than an Archbishop, he was a moral compass, a fearless champion of justice and a global beacon of hope,” notes a release. “ Tutu is a powerful feature documentary that reveals the man behind the iconic voice through never-before-seen archival footage and first-hand accounts from those who walked beside him. The film traces Tutu’s rise as the unwavering voice of the oppressed.

Watch on Deadline

“But behind the public figure and global icon lies an intimate love story: the extraordinary partnership between Desmond and Leah Tutu. In the face of brutality, he stood resolute, guided by faith, fueled by hope and driven by an unshakable belief in the humanity of all people. At its heart, this is a story of the transformative power of forgiveness, a message from which Tutu never wavered.”

Pollard’s directing credits include The Lorraine ; MLK/FBI ; Lowndes County and the Road to Black Power (co-directed with Geeta Gandbhir; Citizen Ashe (co-directed with Rex Miller); Sammy Davis, Jr.: I’ve Gotta Be Me , and many other films. He earned an Oscar nomination for producing the 1997 documentary 4 Little Girls , directed by Spike Lee, and he served as executive producer on The Perfect Neighbor , directed by Geeta Gandbhir, which earned an Academy Award nomination earlier this year.

Pollard said of Tutu , “This film is my way of bringing audiences an intimate portrait that allows Desmond Tutu to speak directly to viewers in his own words and on his own terms. I wanted Tutu’s voice to be the heartbeat of the story, to let his humanity, humor and moral conviction lead us through his world. Working with the remarkable footage captured by filmmakers like Roger Friedman and Benny Gool, who spent over two decades with Tutu, we discovered an extraordinary intimacy. Through their lens, we could step into Tutu’s inner life: his faith and fragility, his joy and the weight he carried beneath it.”

Tutu is produced by Emmy Award winner Johnny Webb ( Zurawski V. Texas ; How Saba Kept Singing ) for HiddenLight, Emmy nominee Ellie Phillips ( The Million Pound Shaman Scam ) and Beya Kabelu. Paul Trewartha ( Kerouac’s Road: The Beat of a Nation ; Don’t Die: The Man Who Wants To Live Forever ; Branson ) is story producer and editor. Executive producers include Sam Pollard, Ricardo Pollack, Niclas Kjellström Matseke (Chairman of The Desmond & Leah Tutu Legacy Foundation), Richard Branson, Sam Branson, Cristina Ljungberg, Dr. Kop Matseke, Dr. Ayanda Ntsaluba, Jens von Bahr, Shannon Sedgwick Davis, Universal Pictures Content Group, and Trevor Noah and Sanaz Yamin for Day Zero Productions.

At the Berlin Film Festival in February, where Tutu held its world premiere, Pollard told Deadline, “[Archibishop Tutu] was going to challenge the status quo in South Africa — always. He wasn’t going to stand by and let things just continue the way they had been for so many years and decades. And he wasn’t saying that he wanted violence, but he was like Dr. King. He was a man who knew that the impact and the importance of non-violent resistance could go a long way in helping a country rid itself with such a racist regime.”

The filmmaker added, “He reached out beyond South Africa globally to Great Britain, to the United States, to basically say, ‘You need to support getting rid of Apartheid in our country.’ And I think part of the fact that he was not only an archbishop, but the Nobel [Peace Prize] laureate helped really have his message reach so many, many places and people.”

"对于第二个问题，吉布尼采用了一种奇怪的导演手法，这威胁到了他那目的明确的批判。他创造了一个阴森森的AI马斯克化身——坐在游戏椅上，身穿皮夹克，头部略显过大——来进行“采访”。虽然AI马斯克说出的所有台词都来自他无数次采访的录音，但这依然是一个奇怪且令人分心的选择。这也是影片反复回归的一个处理方式，主要被用作对吉布尼拉出的那些批评者的反驳：主要是前同事、前浪漫伴侣和记者。这种视觉上的执念进一步加剧了这种效果，它执意将世界重新想象成一种类似《黑客帝国》（Matrix）的模拟，其中他对财富的获取被描绘成在电子游戏中升级。虽然这很符合马斯克对模拟假说的沉思，但它仍然是一个让人分心且不断引人注目的选择。", That’s because for all his talk of AI, self-driving cars, and colonizing Mars, Elon Musk is a frighteningly simple person to decipher. article_text:
A dense, probing, ultimately terrifying exploration of the world’s richest man, Alex Gibney’s four-hour opus Musk isn’t going to reveal anything new about the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX that you couldn’t glean from the myriad books, podcasts, and articles. There’s no smoking gun to explain his laser-like focus on domination or even his intense rightward political shift in recent years. Yet in sweeping across Musk’s life since about 1995—when he founded his first company, Zip2—Gibney nevertheless paints a damning picture in its totality and simplicity. That’s because for all his talk of AI, self-driving cars, and colonizing Mars, Elon Musk is a frighteningly simple person to decipher. The illusion of wealth, status, and brilliance that he carried through the 1990s finally gave way to actual wealth and status by hustling and grifting his way into a succession of companies that were already marginally successful.

You tell enough people that you’re an engineer, eventually they’ll start believing you. Thus Gibney is forced to confront two problems head-on. The first being that, as a psychological portrait, it’s not going to take four hours to explain Elon Musk. He may have immense wealth and power but, as Kara Swisher explains ad nauseum in the film, he’s essentially a child who doesn’t take kindly to being belittled. The second is that, as an ill-fated Twitter (or, as I suppose we have to call it now, X) exchange that begins the film explains, Musk was unwilling to talk to Gibney. Musk calls Gibney a “douche” and Gibney responds “douché,” effectively tanking any prospects of a sit-down.

For the first problem, Gibney wisely doesn’t try to complicate Musk. Instead the filmmaker has overwhelmed with anecdotes and evidence that prove a central thesis: Musk’s base impulses are to take credit for things he didn’t create and obfuscate when they go wrong. He’s a power-hungry oligarch and charlatan who is willing to pull every lever possible to achieve total control, if only to prove he’s the smartest guy in the room.

For the second, Gibney deploys a strange directional affectation that threatens to derail his purposeful critique. He creates a ghoulish AI Musk avatar—sitting in a gamer chair, dressed in a leather jacket, with a head that’s just a little too big—to “interview.” While all the words coming out of AI Musk are recordings from his countless interviews, it’s nevertheless a strange, distracting choice. It’s also one that the film returns to constantly, deployed as a rebuttal to the critics who Gibney trots out: former colleagues, romantic partners, and journalists, mainly. This choice is further compounded by the visual insistence on reimagining the world as a type of Matrix -like simulation where his acquisition of wealth is portrayed as leveling up in a video game. While it may be on-brand with Musk’s musing about the simulation hypothesis, it’s still a distracting choice that constantly calls attention to itself.

More successful is the trove of archival footage that Gibney pulls, beginning all the way back to Zip2 and PayPal, as well as Tesla. There, we see an awkward Musk in oversized dress shirts and a receding hairline before he gradually realized that he needed to look the part of an engineer. While Gibney is less interested in this early era of Musk—dedicating close to half of the entire runtime to Musk’s appalling time running DOGE and supporting right-wing causes under Trump 2.0—it’s nevertheless a fascinating portal into the person he would become. Told almost in its entirety by an interview with Justine Musk, Elon’s first wife, we can see the seeds of Musk’s disengagement with humanity and empathy, as well as the curdling of his relationship with fellow engineers and investors.

From there, Gibney quite rapidly moves through Tesla’s market dominance and woes, circling back to Musk’s claim of an autonomous self-driving car year after year until, eventually, he got something close to it, with the expected disastrous results. We hear from Martin Eberhard, Tesla’s co-founder that Musk eventually pushed out of the company. Yet it’s in the more recent, COVID-era Musk that Gibney seems particularly fascinated. As more than a few commentators suggest, COVID lockdowns triggered a type of break for Musk, who began obsessively pushing conspiracy theories on Twitter and traveling more right in his politics.

After a 10-minute intermission, the second half of Musk is when the horror movie truly begins, as it’s documented how he systematically started aligning himself with conservative figures and became more of a doomsday prepper, complete with an obsession about reproducing his genes. Here, Justine Musk is almost entirely supplanted by Ashley St. Clair, a former conservative influencer and mother of Musk’s son Romulus. St. Clair gives voice to the odd, nefarious ways that Musk exerts control over both his employees and the various mothers of his children through NDAs and monthly stipends. It’s a fascinating, shocking, nauseating dive into a world of legalese. When Trump gains back the White House in 2024, Gibney almost entirely abandons the weird salaciousness of Musk’s personal life to focus on DOGE and the absolute havoc that he and his tween employees wrecked on the federal government.

Of course, what lingers after the film are those who Gibney couldn’t interview. Grimes is oft-discussed but nevertheless a silent victim of Musk’s lack of empathy. His two-time ex-wife Talulah Riley is only given a passing mention. Outside a few former Twitter and U.S. Digital Service employees, we don’t have a full personal accounting of the devastation that his “takeovers” have wrought on those who were on the other end. Yet even with these absences, it nevertheless feels like Gibney has defined the man and distilled him to his basest form. Musk may not go down as the best documentary Alex Gibney has ever made, but it may be his most complete.

Musk is now in theaters.

EXCLUSIVE : A24 ‘s fantasy video game adaptation Elden Ring is heading to the American Film Market, where it’ll be the biggest-budget stand-alone project ever on sale at a film or TV market.

We hear from sources the budget is being pegged between $175 million-$200 million but closer to the latter, which takes the project beyond previous tentpoles that have hit markets, including the latest Hunger Games installment. Mel Gibson’s upcoming Resurrection of the Christ came with a near-$200M price tag but across two films.

Related Stories

Alex Garland’s ‘Elden Ring’ Adaptation At A24 Sets A March 2028 Release In Imax; Cailee Spaeny Among New Additions To Cast

Alex Garland Eyeing Reunion With ‘Warfare’ Actor Kit Connor For His ‘Elden Ring’ Adaptation At A24 & Bandai Namco Entertainment – The Dish

Elden Ring is comfortably A24’s biggest-budget project to date and continues the studio’s trend of taking swings on bigger budgets.

Currently in post, the Alex Garland -scripted and -directed action epic is the talk of the acquisitions community given its scale and ambition. We can reveal today that Amazon MGM Studios has pre-empted that interest by taking a bunch of international pay-1 streaming rights off the table in a big deal. The pact is understood to cover a large number of international markets, and sources speculate to us that it is easily worth tens of millions of dollars. We hear the deal could also potentially lead to interesting activations on Amazon’s Twitch platform.

Watch on Deadline

Amazon is a natural partner for the project given its previous Lord of the Rings investment and flexibility when it comes to international dealmaking. A24, which is fully financing the movie, will have needed/wanted at least one studio partner at that budget. Some international buyers may be disappointed that all-rights aren’t on the table, but their risk now lessens. All-rights asking prices at that budget would have likely been record-breaking and eye-watering.

The Elden Ring cast includes Kit Connor , Ben Whishaw, Cailee Spaeny, Tom Burke, Havana Rose Liu, Sonoya Mizuno, Jonathan Pryce, Ruby Cruz and Nick Offerman. The A-list creative team includes costume designer Jenny Beavan, hair and makeup designer Paul Gooch, and production designers Mark Digby and Michelle Day. David J Thompson is DoP.

Garland wrapped over the summer and is now in post with Industrial Light & Magic. Release is set for March 2028 in theaters and Imax.

The script has been closely guarded in the period leading up to next month’s AFM in Los Angeles in ways generally reserved for the biggest IP. In what seems to be an industry first, A24 is flying members of its team directly to international buyers for them to read the script with the staffer present. It’s a long read; we hear it runs to at least 180 pages with visuals, implying the movie could push towards three hours.

While plot details are largely being kept under wraps, we understand that in-demand Heartstopper actor Connor is the protagonist and the “faithful” film will follow his journey. There are said to be battles between his character and impressive monsters and dragons. But such is the secrecy around the project that parts of the script are being held back from buyers in what is presumably a bid to avoid spoilers and increase intrigue. There is due to be some kind of presentation at the AFM, potentially with footage.

Released to critical acclaim in 2022, the role-playing game from Japanese publisher Bandai Namco is set in a dark fantasy world and allows players to head off on adventures within vast environments and dungeons. The main aim is to journey across “The Lands Between” to defeat the corrupted demigods (known as Shardbearers) and repair the shattered Elden Ring to become the Elden Lord. Created under the guidance of FromSoftware’s Hidetaka Miyazaki, the game is based on a story written by Game of Thrones originator George R.R. Martin.

Newly minted Netflix CCO Peter Rice is producing the movie alongside Andrew Macdonald and Allon Reich from DNA, as well as Martin and Vince Gerardis.

Since its release, the game has sold more than 30 million copies worldwide and received dozens of awards. It ranks among the highest-rated games of all time and had one of the biggest debuts in Twitch history.

The expectation from sources we’ve spoken to, and on fan forums, is that if the movie goes well, there would likely be a sequel; it’s prime fare to become a franchise. But that’s a long way down the line and we’ve heard nothing so far about a sequel being in the works. Elden Ring would need to make a lot of money for that to come to pass. Garland and A24 are first teaming on a Zendaya sci-fi film due to shoot in 2027.

Meanwhile, the fast-ascending Connor is on course to have Elden Ring and the next X-Men movie — he is set to play Cyclops — both releasing in 2028, which could catapult him to tier 1 stardom.

A24, Amazon and producers declined comment.

article_text:
Sequência tem estreia prevista para junho de 2028.

Um dos clássicos entre os filmes de corrida, “ Dias de Trovão ” vai ganhar sequência. O anúncio vem do próprio Tom Cruise , que retoma o papel de Cole Trickle, através de suas redes. Ele confirmou também a escalação de Anne Hathaway e a data de estreia: 2 de junho de 2028 .

Veja o anúncio abaixo.

Days of Thunder. Summer 2028. pic.twitter.com/rD3QLXfUyi — Tom Cruise (@TomCruise) August 29, 2026

Além do anúncio, foi divulgada também a primeira imagem oficial de Cruise e Hathaway divulgando o projeto.

“Dias de Trovão”, lançado em 1990 e dirigido pelo saudoso Tony Scott, tinha Cruise no papel de Cole Trickle, um piloto estreante e impulsivo de stock car que ingressa na NASCAR e precisa superar desafios pessoais e profissionais para alcançar o sucesso. Durante a produção, Cruise conheceu Nicole Kidman, que interpretou seu par romântico; a dupla ainda viria a se casar e estrelar os filmes “Um Sonho Distante” e “De Olhos Bem Fechados”.

A sequência ainda não tem uma trama confirmada, sabendo-se apenas que Anne Hathaway deve interpretar uma proprietária de equipe e engenheira. A direção do novo filme será de Jonathan Levine, com roteiro de Will Staples e produção de Cruise junto a Jerry Bruckheimer e Tommy Harper.

article_text:
Cannes Palme d’Or winner and Oscar nominee Jafar Panahi appears to be caught once again in the crosshairs of the Iranian authorities.

Local media have reported that the director, who spent much of 2025 and early 2026 outside of Iran on the awards trail with It Was Just Sent An Accident , had been given a five-year, one-month prison sentence.

His lawyer Mostafa Nili told Emtedad News Agency that Branch 26 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court had also issued an order for the confiscation of Panahi’s possessions and assets, and slapped him with two-year social media and travel bans.

The lawyer said Panahi discovered that court hearings were underway against him after his bank accounts were frozen out of the blue.

Nili and his client paid a visit to the Sentence Enforcement Unit of the Culture and Media Prosecutor’s Office, where they learned that Panahi had been convicted “in absentia” in a separate case.

The director currently has three open cases in Iran but according to Nili had not been officially summoned for hearings, even though he is in the country.

The new sentence comes on top of a separate one-year prison sentence and a two-year travel meted out by the Iranian Branch 26 court in 2025, on charges of “propaganda activities against the system.”

Panahi has long been in the crosshairs of Iran’s hardline Islamic Republic authorities. He spent seven months in the country’s Evin jail after being arrested in July 2022 after. Iranian authorities reactivated a six-year sentence originally meted out to Panahi in 2010 alongside a 20-year filmmaking and travel ban.

He had originally gone to the prison to enquire about the whereabouts of fellow filmmakers Mohammad Rasoulof and Mostafa Al-Ahmad who had been arrested a few days previously for criticizing the actions of the authorities in an open letter.

The reactivated sentence were connected to Panahi’s attendance of a funeral in 2009 of a student shot dead in the Green Revolution and his later attempt to shoot a feature set against the backdrop of the uprising. He was released in February 2023 after going on hunger strike.

It seemed for a time that the authorities were softening their stance towards the director after he was granted permission to travel to Cannes for the first time in 15 years in 2025 for the premiere of clandestinely shot film It Was Just An Accident . It went on to win the Palme d’Or and then be Oscar nominated in the Best International Feature Film Category as the French entry.

While on the final stages of awards campaign trail, Panahi publicly denounced a deadly crackdown on pro-democracy protests which swept Iran in January 2026 in which tens of thousands are believe to have died.

In spite of the tense political situation in Iran and potential threat to his own freedom, Panahi vowed to return home as soon as his Oscar contender duties were done and dusted, which he did.

article_text:
There is a scene in Noah Baumbach’s Jay Kelly (2025) in which the eponymous movie star—an industrially entrenched A-lister who’s entered the “lifetime-achievement award” phase of his brilliant career—stands in front of a bathroom mirror. There, he recites the names of other great leading men one after another, alongside his own: “Gary Cooper. Cary Grant. Jay Kelly. Clark Gable. Jay Kelly. Robert De Niro. Jay Kelly.” The words sound like a mantra, or an incantation. To paraphrase Travis Bickle, are they talking to him, or he to them? The anxiety of influence is a doppelgänger for delusions of grandeur. When you stare at the abyss, it (navel-)gazes back at you.

Conspicuous by its absence on Jay’s short list of Hollywood royalty is the name “George Clooney.” The joke is that Clooney is also extremely conspicuous in this scene by his presence. This would be true even if he weren’t playing a character in Jay Kelly modeled—however indirectly, and with plenty of playful humor and room for plausible deniability—on his own celebrity. “It’s a hell of a responsibility to be yourself,” reads an opening title card attributed to Sylvia Plath, although a quote from Bruce Wayne in Batman & Robin (1997) could also work as an epigram, for both Jay Kelly’s wild strawberries–flavored journey down memory lane and Jay Kelly ’s melancholy showbiz metaphysics: “To succeed, we need only pick a star and follow it.”

For the record: George Clooney is not Cary Grant, nor Gary Cooper, nor his hero and onetime confidant Paul Newman, though he surely follows them. He isn’t Jay Kelly either, even if they seem to have appeared in many of the same movies. What Clooney is is conspicuous, always. His reputation, like his jawline, precedes him. When Time called him “The Last Movie Star” back in 2008, it was somehow premature and prescient at the same time, an acknowledgment of larger shifts in both the Hollywood hierarchy and celebrity culture at large. Hence the subtext of Clooney’s aging-apex-predator act in Wolfs (2024), a comic thriller about shady underworld types pressurized by themes of professional obsolescence and incipient extinction. “I just wanted to see how an old man would do it,” snarks Brad Pitt’s nameless cipher to Clooney’s similarly anonymous opposite number. Clooney’s spirit animal is increasingly the wily coyote, or maybe the alpha dog who fears he’s part of a vanishing breed. But as Jay Kelly proves—not that anyone was arguing the point—if there’s one thing he can’t do as an actor, it’s disappear.

Which is not to say that he’s incapable of magic tricks. In the right roles, Clooney channels that aforementioned conspicuousness—that heightened quality of recognizability—into a kind of flesh-and-blood special effect. Pauline Kael, who shouted out Clooney’s performance in Three Kings (1999) in her final on-the-record interview (“he was very good”), once called Cary Grant “The Man From Dream City.” Clooney’s gifts put that phrase in reverse. Instead of materializing out of thin air, he’s grounded, earthbound—not a figure of fantasy but a stickler for mischief. “Is this your first time being robbed? You’re doing great,” purrs stickup-expert Jack Foley to a mesmerized female bank teller in Steven Soderbergh’s heist thriller Out of Sight (1998); he turns armed robbery into a come-on. Tasked consistently with playing petty thieves, swindlers, and ethically flexible professional types, Clooney traverses familiar actorly terrain and transforms it, by sheer force of presence.

We want to look at some actors because their beauty is an open book, or a glossy magazine cover. Clooney, though, holds our gaze by concealment; his eyes are like tinted windows to the soul. To invert Kael on Grant, his face muscles never betray him, but they tell on his characters all the time, in increments. Exhibit A: Michael Clayton in the back seat of that taxi cab, an escape artist in a trap of his own making, held hostage by a close-up shot that refuses to cut to black. It’s telling, perhaps, that Clooney excels in roles that require his characters to keep up appearances. Exhibit B: his anguished CIA whistleblower Bob Barnes in Syriana (2005), who’s described by his own son as a “professional liar.” Who else would volunteer to play the hapless, just-following-orders bomber pilot commanded to drop the big one in Stephen Frears’s Fail Safe (2000), a live-to-air network-TV remake of Sidney Lumet’s Fail Safe (1964)? Clooney has often said that one of his favorite movies is Network (1976), which observes falling skies from ground level. One gets the feeling that if Clooney—who decided that what he really wanted to do was direct with 2002’s CIA-themed comedy Confessions of a Dangerous Mind —could have been any American filmmaker other than himself, it would have been Lumet.

Or maybe he’d have been one of the Coen Brothers. Both Confessions and the knockabout football farce Leatherheads (2008) betray the influence of Joel and Ethan. The pleasure of Clooney’s performances for the Coens lies in how thoroughly he punctures his own bubble, so that the gravitas escapes. Clooney doesn’t ever disappear, but in these films, he is a shape-shifter. Long before Jay Kelly wondered how he stacked up against the star of It Happened One Night (1934), Clooney did a spot-on impersonation of Clark Gable in O Brother, Where Art Thou? (2000). Beyond its merits as an old-timey picaresque, that film began an extended and rewarding tradition of the siblings kidding their leading man’s vanity. Notable examples: con man Ulysses Everett McGill’s Dapper Dan pomade dependency in O Brother , star divorce attorney Miles Massey’s nuclear-bleached chompers in Intolerable Cruelty (2003), and U.S. Marshal Harry Pfarrer’s nervous tics in Burn After Reading (2008). Pfarrer’s cloak-and-dagger paranoia plays like a satirical revamp of Syriana , right down to Clooney’s beard. Instead of getting strapped into a chair by his enemies, Clooney’s character in Burn After Reading proudly shows off his own customized homemade sex throne, a just-for-her-pleasure endeavor kitted out with a store-bought dildo. (“I’m not set up to mold hard rubber,” he explains while gazing admiringly at his handiwork.)

“”Every time they send me a script, they say ‘you’re going to play a knucklehead’,” Clooney claimed of Joel and Ethan during the press tour for Hail, Caesar! (2016), in which he plays a hilariously suggestible 1950s matinee idol being force-fed dialectics by a cabal of left-leaning screenwriters. It’s a great piece of casting, effectively transforming Clooney into a liberal caricature worthy, if that’s the right word, of his haters. “Can’t [Clooney] see what the Coens are up to?” wondered Armond White, sardonically noting the conceptual links between Hail, Caesar! ’s Blacklist-era pastiche and Clooney’s sophomore directorial effort Good Night, and Good Luck. (2005), about the public battle between Edward R. Murrow and Joseph McCarthy. A better question might be how somebody could miss the wicked self-deprecation of Clooney’s turn as Baird Whitlock in Hail, Caesar! (“What if I name names?” he queries his captors craftily).

Where Confessions of a Dangerous Mind spoofed cloak-and-dagger tropes, Good Night, and Good Luck. felt at the time like an extension of Clooney’s still-fervent activism. It’s every bit as square-jawed and sincere in its evocation of postwar Pax Americana as Hail, Caesar! is wild and woolly. This media-class morality play unfolds handsomely, classically, in (literal) black and white. It’s a solid (not stolid) and thoughtful movie that shows Clooney the director displaying a mix of visual acuity and self-effacement. As CBS producer Fred Friendly, he cuts a dashing, chiaroscuro figure while generously ceding the movie to David Strathairn’s Murrow, secure enough in his stardom to give a supporting performance. There are other examples: one reason why Alfonso Cuarón’s Gravity (2013) gains propulsion as a proverbial one-woman show for Sandra Bullock is that Clooney ensures something is at stake in his own character’s expendability (“Sit back, enjoy the ride,” he says before floating off into space, a benediction not just to Bullock’s character, but also the audience).

It’s telling that for all the Clooney movies that hinge on the premise of actor-as-event—not just Michael Clayton and Jay Kelly , but also Up in the Air (2009) and The Descendants (2011)—he’s often most effective in ensembles. The Ocean’s trilogy (2001-07) is the obvious example, with each successive entry more crowded with stars and more egalitarian, but there’s also David O. Russell’s Gulf War action comedy Three Kings , reportedly produced under duress but still maybe the most persuasive showcase, along with Out of Sight , of the actor’s ability to give even halfway-decent comic dialogue some Pete Sampras–level topspin. “That’s what makes SF so badass,” scoffs Clooney’s insubordinate Special Forces honcho Archie Gates, who turns his tour of duty in Iraq into a treasure hunt. “We got the best flashlights.”

Three Kings ’s Altmanesque, war-is-hell horror show puts Clooney’s entire leading-man package on display: the skeptically arched eyebrows; the withering, sidelong one-liners; the tarnished-angel charisma; and the implicit sense of social conscience. The film looks in retrospect like the primal scene of Clooney’s screen persona, as well as of the criticism—lobbed plenty of times in real life, and as a rhetorical boomerang skittering through Jay Kelly ’s house of mirrors—that Clooney’s range is perilously narrow, that he specializes in mediated self-portraiture. His response to these observations has historically been succinct: “I don’t give a shit,” he told Vanity Fair , protesting not too much but just enough, implying (without coming out and saying so) that making things look easy isn’t so easy.

Which means, of course, that he does give a shit—about the work, if not how it’s perceived. The final shot of Michael Clayton distills this tension. It works because of how assiduously Clooney works to bypass the fourth wall without quite breaking it. He has the expression of a man resigned to looking over his shoulder in perpetuity (the scene was shot in the middle of Manhattan, amidst a throng of real-life rubberneckers). Michael glances above, askance at, and past the camera, past us, towards some imagined vanishing point. If it’s possible to act in high-definition while blurring the edges, Clooney makes it happen. He’s his own rack focus. Somewhere, an actor wondering if he’s ready for his own sustained close-up will think of this scene while looking in the mirror; the name on his lips may or may not go without saying.

article_text:
Films and events

Laugh

Relaxed screening: The History of Concrete

Relaxed screenings

House lights will remain on a low level throughout the screening, and the volume will be turned down. Audience members will be able to make noise, stim freely, move around or leave and return during the screening.

We will provide a sanctuary space for you to use near the auditorium.

See other screenings of this film

Having attended a Hallmark movie workshop, John Wilson applies his learnings to a documentary about concrete, albeit with a dryly funny and deceptively understated tone.

Credits

Director John Wilson

USA 2026. 101min

Courtesy of Visit Films

Language English

Access information

Wednesday 14 October 20:35

Relaxed screening

Descriptive subtitles

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

After finding himself with too much time on his hands, documentarian Wilson attends a workshop on how to make Hallmark romcoms. It inspires him to apply the formula to a film investigating the story of concrete. Infused with Wilson’s trademark curiosity and wit, the film project introduces him to a variety of unusual people and places. The result is a wry and humane meditation on the modern world.

Chloé Trayner

Content advice

Contains ableist attitudes and language.

Before the screening

Doors will open 30 minutes before the screening start time.

No trailers will be shown.

The programme will be introduced.

During the screening

Our house lights will remain on a low level throughout the screening, and the volume will be turned slightly down.

You will be able to leave the auditorium and return during the screening.

You will be able to make noise.

We will provide a quiet space for you to use near the auditorium.

You are welcome to take refreshments into the cinema but no hot food please. For information on BFI Bar & Kitchen and BFI Riverfront please see our food and drink page .

How to book

Find out about booking access tickets .

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

editorial_excerpt_zh: 在英国提交其迟交的 2024 年账目几天后，Pace 已提交其 2025 年报告。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "在英国提交其迟交的 2024 年账目几天后，Pace 已提交其 2025 年报告，显示其国际业务去年亏损 560 万美元。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些文件提交给了英国政府的公司注册处（Companies House），这是负责维护在英国注册的企业的年度记录的部门。这些文件仅涵盖帕斯画廊有限公司（The Pace Gallery Limited），这是一家在伦敦注册的公司，负责运营画廊的伦敦空间，并拥有其在香港、北京、首尔、日内瓦和柏林的子公司。Pace 的美国业务未被包括在内。", "links": [{"text": "filed with Companies House", "url": "https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/07117911/filing-history"}, {"text": "Pace Gallery", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/pace-gallery/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2025 年的文件显示，营业额（英国对收入的称呼）为 6590 万美元。这明显低于 2023 年的 1.049 亿美元，但仅比 2024 年的 6770 万美元略低。盈利能力下降得更为剧烈。尽管收入略有下降，但销售成本却上升了 12%，毛利润下降了 740 万美元，降至 1280 万美元。截至年底的现金余额也持续下降，从 2023 年的 3480 万美元降至 2024 年的 2410 万美元，再到 2025 年的 1110 万美元。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些数字解释了帕斯画廊在 6 月决定从其阵容中剔除约 50 位艺术家并全球裁员约 50 人的决定。当时，《金融时报》报道称，该画廊位于汉诺威广场的伦敦空间正在出售，而画廊正在考虑搬到更靠近大卫·齐弗纳（David Zwirner）的较小地点。", "links": [{"text": "Pace’s decision in June", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/pace-gallery-layoffs-artist-roster-cuts-1234788318/"}, {"text": "reported", "url": "https://www.ft.com/content/5c661326-0e44-4f74-a63c-40a474fbf923"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些文件直接描述了削减成本的计划，称画廊减少了阵容，削减了“全职支持职位的数量”，并缩减了 2026 年夏季的展览。文件中并未列出受影响的国际员工人数。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "新提交的文件也紧随记者朱莉·布伦纳·达维奇（Julie Brener Davich）对画廊的三部分调查之后，该调查详细披露了“关于‘轻率’高管支出的指控”。尽管首席执行官马克·格利姆彻（Marc Glimcher）告诉布伦纳·达维奇，画廊并未在“荒谬和浪费的事项”上花钱，但她报道称，画廊频繁使用私人飞机来吸引艺术家和客户，以及由豪华顾问亚历山大·吉尔克斯（Alexander Gilkes）主导的办公室翻新，后者倡议在每层楼安装价值 1.2 万美元的咖啡机，并在冰箱里备有康普茶和 12 美元一瓶的矿泉水。", "links": [{"text": "Brener Davich", "url": "https://juliebdavich.substack.com/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在两份文件中，画廊表示其国际业务“依赖于母公司《Pace Gallery LLC》的财务支持”，这家位于纽约的母公司向英国公司的董事提供了“保证”，“包括马克·格利姆彻和阿恩·格利姆彻”，即支持将继续，并且“在账目获批之日起至少12个月内，他们不会寻求偿还应付给他们的资金”，除非所有第三方债务均已清偿。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "文件还指出，美国母公司计划在2026年底之前通过发行新股，将对英国公司的欠款转换为股权。截至去年年底，英国公司欠其母公司2130万美元。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Pace的一位发言人向Artnet News表示，这一举措是“更广泛的全球财务管理策略的一部分”，不应被解读为“英国业务的亏损或流动性问题”。此举旨在“加强英国公司的资产负债表”。", "links": [{"text": "a statement to Artnet News", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/market/pace-uk-2025-financials-2829690"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Pace尚未对ARTnews的评论请求作出回应。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是一则正在发展的新闻，将不断更新。", "translated": true}]

They cover only The Pace Gallery Limited, the London-registered company that operates the gallery’s London space and owns its subsidiaries in Hong Kong, Beijing, Seoul, Geneva, and Berlin. Pace’s US operations are not included.", "links": [{"text": "filed with Companies House", "url": "https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/07117911/filing-history"}, {"text": "Pace Gallery", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/pace-gallery/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The 2025 filing shows that turnover—the UK term for revenue—was $65.9 million. That is well below 2023’s $104.9 million, but only a shade lower than 2024’s $67.7 million. Profitability fell much more sharply. Cost of sales rose 12 percent even as revenue slipped, and gross profit dropped by $7.4 million, to $12.8 million. Cash on hand at year end has also kept falling, from $34.8 million in 2023 to $24.1 million in 2024 and $11.1 million in 2025."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The figures help explain Pace’s decision in June to drop some 50 artists from its roster and lay off about 50 staff members globally. At the time, the Financial Times reported that the gallery’s London space in Hanover Square is on the market and that the gallery is eyeing a smaller location closer to David Zwirner.", "links": [{"text": "Pace’s decision in June", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/pace-gallery-layoffs-artist-roster-cuts-1234788318/"}, {"text": "reported", "url": "https://www.ft.com/content/5c661326-0e44-4f74-a63c-40a474fbf923"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The filings describe that cost-cutting plan directly, saying the gallery reduced its roster, cut “the number of full-time support roles,” and scaled back exhibitions in summer 2026. Just days after filing its long-delayed 2024 accounts in the UK, Pace has filed its 2025 report, showing that its international business posted a $5.6 million loss last year.

The documents were filed with Companies House , the branch of the UK government that maintains annual records for businesses established there. They cover only The Pace Gallery Limited, the London-registered company that operates the gallery’s London space and owns its subsidiaries in Hong Kong, Beijing, Seoul, Geneva, and Berlin. Pace’s US operations are not included.

The 2025 filing shows that turnover—the UK term for revenue—was $65.9 million. That is well below 2023’s $104.9 million, but only a shade lower than 2024’s $67.7 million. Profitability fell much more sharply. Cost of sales rose 12 percent even as revenue slipped, and gross profit dropped by $7.4 million, to $12.8 million. Cash on hand at year end has also kept falling, from $34.8 million in 2023 to $24.1 million in 2024 and $11.1 million in 2025.

The figures help explain Pace’s decision in June to drop some 50 artists from its roster and lay off about 50 staff members globally. At the time, the Financial Times reported that the gallery’s London space in Hanover Square is on the market and that the gallery is eyeing a smaller location closer to David Zwirner.

The filings describe that cost-cutting plan directly, saying the gallery reduced its roster, cut “the number of full-time support roles,” and scaled back exhibitions in summer 2026. The number of international staffers affected is not outlined in the documents.

The new filings also come on the heels of journalist Julie Brener Davich’s three-part investigation into the gallery, which detailed “claims of ‘reckless’ executive spending.” While CEO Marc Glimcher told Brener Davich that the gallery had not spent on “frivolous and wasteful things,” she reported frequent use of a private jet to court artists and clients, as well as an office revamp led by luxury consultant Alexander Gilkes, at whose initiative the gallery installed $12,000 coffee machines on each floor and stocked fridges with kombucha and $12 bottles of water.

In both filings, the gallery says the international business is “dependent on financial support” from The Pace Gallery LLC, its New York–based parent company. The UK company’s directors have “received assurances” from the parent, “together with Marc Glimcher and Arne Glimcher,” that support will continue and that they “will not seek repayment of monies due to them for at least 12 months” from the date the accounts were approved, unless all third-party liabilities have been met.

The filings also state that the US parent intends to convert the money it is owed by the UK company into equity, through the issue of new shares, by the end of 2026. At the end of last year, the UK company owed its parent $21.3 million.

In a statement to Artnet News , a Pace spokesperson characterized the conversation as part of “a broader global financial management strategy” that should not be interpreted as “a loss or liquidity issue for the UK business.” The conversation is intended to “strengthen the UK company’s balance sheet.”

Pace has yet to respond to a request for comment from ARTnews .

This is a developing story and will be updated.

自画像 47KMの夢

劇場公開日： 2026年11月10日

解説・あらすじ

中国・湖北省の農村に毎年通い、村の人々と自身の変化を記録し続けるジャン・モンチーのドキュメンタリー「自画像 47KM」シリーズの第3作。村に関わろうとする監督の試みと空回りを、自身のパフォーマンスも交えて描いた。 2010年、大学を出たばかりのジャン・モンチーは、老人たちへの聞き取りのため、父の故郷である「47KM村」と呼ばれる村を訪れた。それから毎年村に通い続ける監督は、やがて村に図書室を作ろうと考える。子どもたちを集めてゴミ拾いの活動も始めるが、周囲の大人たちからは子どもに関わるなと反対されてしまう。貧しい暮らしをする老女の家に電線を引こうとすれば、嫁に怒られるからやめてほしいと断られる。村に貢献したいという思いは、行き場を失っていく。 ジャン・モンチーは1987年、中国湖北省生まれ。中央民族大学でダンスを学び、ダンサーや振付家として活動しながら2010年に村での撮影を始め、2020年には村に家を建てて移り住んだ。本作は、シリーズ10作を一挙上映する「ジャン・モンチー監督 47KMシリーズ特集上映」（2026年11月7～20日＝ポレポレ東中野）で日本初上映される。
